llm.summary: The SKILL.md describes a local gateway + cloud detection product that requires installing and running code, but the published skill is instruction-only (no install, no code, no declared file/credential access), so the package's claims and its actual registry footprint don't line up.

dimensions.detail: The description promises a runtime security plugin that runs a local gateway (localhost:38790), hooks into OpenClaw events, and sends sanitized metadata to a cloud detection service. However the registry entry contains no install spec, no code files, no required binaries, and no required config paths — meaning the skill as published cannot by itself provide the claimed local daemon or hooks. The SKILL.md repeatedly references an npm package (@openguardrails/moltguard) and GitHub source, which implies external installation is required but that is not reflected in the skill manifest.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: The instructions describe event hooks that read tool calls and possibly filesystem paths (sensitive file categories, credentials path) and describe registration/activation network calls. The SKILL.md also instructs users to run npm/tar commands to verify package provenance. Because the skill is instruction-only, those runtime behaviors (reading files, registering, activating) are not enforced or implemented here — the document grants broad authority in principle but lacks concrete, self-contained implementation, creating ambiguity about what will actually run and where data might go.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (lowest surface area). However the SKILL.md repeatedly references an npm package and shows npm/tar verification commands; it assumes you will install @openguardrails/moltguard from npm or GitHub. That external install step is not automated or declared in the registry entry, so users would need to fetch and run third-party code themselves. The absence of an embedded install makes the registry entry itself low-risk, but it also means the document's claims rely on out-of-band installation that the registry does not control or audit.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill declares no required environment variables or config paths, yet the documentation references storing credentials at ~/.openclaw/credentials/moltguard/credentials.json, reading many sensitive file categories (SSH keys, AWS creds, browser cookies, etc.), and sending sanitized metadata to openguardrails.com. There is a mismatch: the skill asks for no secrets up front but describes behavior that will interact with sensitive data if the external package is installed. This lack of declared required access is an incoherence and reduces transparency about privileges needed.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The registry flags are default (always:false), which is appropriate. The SKILL.md describes registration, activation, and storing an agent ID/api key locally for billing/usage — persistent data written to ~/.openclaw/credentials/... would be created by the external package. That persistence is not represented in the skill manifest; users should be aware activation triggers network calls and local credential storage if they install the package.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This published skill is essentially documentation about an external product rather than a self-contained plugin. Before trusting or installing anything: 1) Don't assume the registry entry provides runtime protection — the SKILL.md expects you to install @openguardrails/moltguard from npm/GitHub. 2) Inspect the actual package source/tarball and compare it to the GitHub repo (the SKILL.md even provides diff steps) before installing. 3) Verify the local gateway genuinely runs on localhost:38790 and observe network traffic (tcpdump/mitmproxy/Little Snitch) to confirm only sanitized metadata is sent to openguardrails.com. 4) Run the package in a sandbox (container or VM) and with least privilege; check file writes (credentials path) and permissions (0600). 5) If you need strict assurance, ask the publisher for a signed release or reproducible build; absence of an install spec in the registry is a red flag — treat this as a pointer to external software, not a ready-to-run skill. If you want, provide the npm package tarball or the GitHub commit/tag you plan to install and I can re-evaluate the code-level risk.
